thread.title: Pandora Is Copying YouTube, Not Spotify. And It's Working - Pandora Media (NYSE:P)

author: Max Greve
title: Pandora Is Copying YouTube, Not Spotify. And It's Working - Pandora Media (NYSE:P)
text:
For the first time in a long time, I don’t have to hang my head in shame when I tell people I’m a Pandora (NYSE: P ) bull. The stock, worn down by years of competition with Spotify (NYSE: SPOT ) and Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), is finally showing signs of life, bouncing 40% this month following earnings to back above $7. Although I first went long at $11, continuing purchases as I followed it down cut my cost basis below $6, meaning I am now in the black.
Many contributors have focused since the announcement on Pandora’s subscription services or its AdsWizz acquisition as powering the stock’s nascent comeback. I cannot speak to the motivations of Street buyers, but in my opinion, the improvements in Pandora’s fundamentals, while real, do not stem from these factors. At least not yet. I was betting on something else when I stayed long the stock, and so far it seems to be working out. Pandora is taking a page out of Google's ( GOOG , GOOGL) YouTube book.
Subscription Shortfalls Let me dispose of the subscription angle first. Yes, Pandora reported a sharp uptick in subscription revenue, but that is more than offset by the concurrent increase in subscription costs. As I’ve noted before, the company committed to minimum guaranteed content payments to music producers when it launched Premium, and so far it has not attracted enough subscribers to meet these thresholds.
The result is that Pandora’s entire subscription revenue from Premium goes right back out the door in content payments, along with some of its own cash to boot to meet the minimums. And all this is before counting all the product development expenses that went into developing Premium in the first place.
I’ve already noted this dynamic in analyzing past earnings, but this time was no different. Perhaps the biggest downside in an otherwise sterling report was that Pandora’s gross margins continued to contract. On the earnings call , CFO Naveen Chopra said that minimum guarantees (MGs) accounted for over 100% of the deterioration in gross margins Y/Y, and that margins would have actually grown absent the MG obligations.
So despite the impressive-sounding percentage growth figure for subscription revenue, it is not the reason Pandora’s bottom line is starting to show signs of improvement. Quite the reverse, in fact.
Audio and AdsWizz If Pandora did not beat by banking on subscription, it must by definition have beaten by banking on advertising. And indeed, this past quarter saw the company’s decision to invest further in programmatic audio through the AdsWizz acquisition, a deal that it finally closed this week . While AdsWizz may well have significance down the road, investors should not fail to note that Pandora’s numbers are already improving, even though the acquisition wasn’t even done last quarter and won’t substantially impact earnings for several more.
But Pandora’s numbers are improving now. So if it's not the audio advertising and it's not the subscription services, what is left?
Premium Access Please note that I was careful with my terminology in the above section. Pandora’s subscription service does not impress me, but that does not mean that I am disappointed to see the company finally securing contracts with content providers for Pandora Premium. As I’ve argued before, Pandora Premium’s biggest impact may be on its free-tier service. I believe last quarter’s numbers have validated my thesis on that front.
Premium Access is the service the company offers to ad-supported listeners to obtain the benefits of Pandora Premium for a brief time in exchange for watching a video ad. This new advertising engine essentially replaces the audio one, since one of the perks of Premium is no ad interruptions.
Pandora built the backbone for it when it launched Sponsored Listening two years ago, which uses a similar active engagement video tool to eliminate audio ads for listeners for a period of 1-4 hours after they have opted to watch a video ad from the sponsor. Sponsored Listening doesn’t offer the other perks of Premium, but it does last longer.
Premium Access Pandora bears have made the decline in the company’s active user metric one of the hallmarks of their case, and rightfully so. But even worse than the number itself has been the fact that Pandora’s listener losses are not scattered randomly throughout its user base. Rather, they are concentrated overwhelmingly in the teen demographic.
But Premium Access has begun to reverse this.
Last month, a Pandora spokesperson gave the first indication that things were going even better than expected. The company said Premium Access had 6.5 million unique users (as of what date wasn’t specified), and they were overweighted towards the 25 and under demographic that has found Spotify so appealing. But as it turns out, that was just a small taste. During the earnings call, Roger Lynch, Pandora's President and CEO, said that number had already grown to 13 million as of date.
Note that this appears to be just Premium Access. Sponsored Listening is a separate service, even though it runs off of the same CPV advertising engine, and may well have millions more unique users.
Pandora's Real Turnaround Chopra referred to these ad revenues as “non-guaranteed,” since advertisers bid for them programmatically instead of signing contracts with Pandora’s sales staff. Chopra also said that they were responsible for the bulk of the outperformance in the company’s ad revenue category - a category which we know performed so well it would have increased Pandora’s total gross margins, were it not for the concomitant performance of its subscription side.
These two statements, taken together, make it very clear what is powering Pandora’s turnaround. It is not subscriptions, which remain in the red and aren’t even really providing notably less drag than they were six months ago. It is not AdsWizz, an acquisition which hadn’t closed yet and which is months away from substantially contributing even now that it has. And it wasn’t traditional radio advertising, where the company continues to underperform, although I have hopes for the future on this front.
It was actually the CPV advertising engine, composed overwhelmingly of visual advertising, including video and digital display. It was also the superior consumer experience this advertising engine powers, which allows for greater consumer control of the music experience and better recommendation engine performance from Pandora when it does take over choosing the next song.
Investment Summary Chopra warned us that because the company doesn’t have much experience with CPV advertising yet, it doesn’t want to make assumptions about it going forward, so it has kept its projections conservative for now. But it seems unlikely that this advertising engine will stall out, given that Pandora, for all its faults, is still one of the largest consumer mobile applications in the US today. Over 70 million Americans interact with Pandora for 25 hours per month, making it one of the best platforms out there to reach consumers. Assuming CPV revenues continue to come in strong, as I believe they will, the company has a new path to eliminating its red ink.
Despite Pandora’s 40% rise this past month, I remain bullish on the stock.
Disclosure: I am/we are long P.
